answers.rationale: FlashAttention stores O(BHN) (m,l) statistics and recomputes P block-by-block in backward — that's A. Naive backward materializes the O(N^2) P/S matrix which dominates activations at long context — that's C. B is wrong: forward+backward re-compute makes total FLOPs strictly larger than forward only, but total (fwd+bwd) FLOPs of FA vs naive is roughly the same order (a small constant more) and the wall-clock win is I/O; the sweeping 'strictly larger than forward-only baseline' misstates baseline. Actually re-read B: it says FLOPs strictly larger than forward-only baseline. That is trivially true — but says wall-clock speedup 'comes entirely from reduced HBM traffic dominating extra compute'; the 'entirely' is a strong claim; FA backward's benefit is HBM I/O reduction — acceptable. Wait — B compares FA backward to forward-only baseline, which is nonsensical (baseline for backward is naive backward, not forward). B is misleading. D is wrong: FA proves you can avoid materializing P in HBM.

im2col replicates by R*S and uses GEMM; same FLOPs as direct conv; im2col uses more memory but leverages tuned GEMM/tensor cores. B/C/D are wrong (im2col doesn't reduce FLOPs; im2col uses more memory not less; the choice affects performance).
Embedding gather: for each of B*N indices, one contiguous row read of D elements. Zero FLOPs; bandwidth-bound. Warps cooperate per row so accesses are coalesced within a row.

Bias-add and elementwise activations fuse cleanly as GEMM epilogue on accumulator tile (B). RMSNorm reduces across the last axis so it typically cannot fuse as a standard elementwise epilogue unless full-row tile — D correctly describes this. A wrong (tensor cores + epilogue is standard). C wrong (RMSNorm is not elementwise; requires reduction).

A: O(N log N) Cooley-Tukey with log-N radix rounds — correct. B: each round is O(N) memory, low intensity, memory-bound — correct. D: FFT-based convolution via convolution theorem is standard for long kernels — correct. C wrong: FFT rounding introduces float error; not bit-exact.
FA is exact math with block-tiled online softmax; backward recomputes attention weights from (m,l) and Q,K,V. B/C/D describe approximations FA does not use.
Naive writes/reads S=[N,N] to HBM; FA keeps S on-chip. FA HBM I/O is O(N^2 d/M) which reduces to ~O(Nd) when tiles fit. A reverses the direction; B/C wrong about I/O reduction being the main benefit.

B: FA backward deliberately recomputes P from stats — correct. C: exact math, same FLOP count — correct. D: HBM I/O scales as O(N^2 d / M) — the standard result. A wrong: no uniform 3-4x speedup; hardware-dependent.

Modern LLM inference kernels typically fuse up+activation (avoiding the [B,N,F] HBM roundtrip within that kernel) and keep down GEMM separate. B (full three-op fusion with K-reduction) is non-standard and complex; C (no fusion) is wrong; D (concat weights) is wrong because up and down don't share output dim.

B: register pressure can hurt occupancy causing spills — correct. C: fusion reduces HBM roundtrips and launch overhead; FLOPs unchanged — correct. D: producer-consumer fusion easy; fusion across reduction requires restructuring — correct. A wrong: fusion is not always beneficial.

Fused QKV is numerically equivalent up to rounding; benefit is single kernel launch and one X read. A/B/C are wrong (no cross-projection coupling; MQA/GQA still fuse with combined [D, D + 2*H_kv*d] weight; doesn't double FLOPs).
Standard tiled GEMM AI ~ M_TILE*N_TILE / (M_TILE+N_TILE); larger tiles amortize A/B fetches, ceiling by register/SMEM. A/B/D wrong.
GEMV: A streamed with no reuse; ~1 flop/byte for FP16, well below ridge; memory-bound. B/C/D wrong.

Grouped GEMM: single kernel launch dispatching per-group tile schedules across SMs; amortizes launch overhead; small groups share SMs. A (Winograd) wrong; B (reduction across experts) wrong; C (batched with padding) is a different approach that wastes work.

A: GQA preserves quality better than MQA, more KV than MQA but less than MHA — standard result. C: KV = 2*G*d per layer; typical G=H/8 or H/4 gives 4-8x reduction — correct. B wrong: GQA can be obtained by mean-pooling KV heads from a pretrained MHA model with light finetuning (uptraining). D wrong: GQA doesn't reduce attention FLOPs — each query head still runs full attention against its group's shared KV.
Prefill writes P KV entries; decode step t writes 1 new entry and reads P+t entries; total decode read is sum ~ O(T*(P+T)*H_kv*d). A/B/C wrong on the read/write pattern.

A: decode is BW-bound on KV reads, KV quantization is a direct lever — correct. B: one new K/V entry written, full cache read — correct. D: MQA/GQA reuse loaded K/V tile across query heads via SMEM staging — correct. C wrong: PagedAttention does NOT have strictly higher HBM latency; block sizes are chosen so accesses remain coalesced.
MHA H_kv=H, MQA H_kv=1, GQA in between; MQA cuts KV BW by H over MHA. A/C/D wrong on the KV head structure.

C: params scale with E but compute per token is roughly constant (top-k activated) plus O(E) gating — the key MoE property. D: load imbalance is real; sqrt(B*N/E) variance under random routing; capacity limits/EP load balancing needed. A wrong: expert parallelism does distribute weight-loading cost across devices. B wrong on the compute-per-token scaling.

Standard top-k MoE dataflow: gate scores over E experts, top-k selected per token, softmax over top-k, only those k experts run, output combined by gate weights; capacity limits/aux losses for load balance.
Standard online softmax merge: m_{t+1}=max(m_t,m'); d_{t+1}= d_t*exp(m_t - m_{t+1}) + d'*exp(m' - m_{t+1}).
Standard warp-shuffle + shared reduction pattern. A/C/D wrong.

A: RMSNorm is BW-bound; O(N) IO with negligible compute per element. B: single reduction of E[x^2], no mean subtraction, fewer ops than LN — correct. C wrong: it's memory bound. D wrong: not identical to LN even at zero mean (there's still the bias term missing and different formulation).
RMSNorm one reduction (sum x^2); LN can be single-pass with E[x^2]-E[x]^2 (two moments); HBM read of x once. C correct; A/B/D wrong.
RoPE rotates feature-dim pairs of Q and K by position-dependent angles; applied elementwise after QKV projection, before QK^T; not applied to V; token-independent rotation. C correct.
Temperature divides logits by T (T>1 flatten, T<1 sharpen) before softmax; top-p sorts descending, keeps smallest set whose cumsum first exceeds p, renormalize. B correct.
Max subtraction makes exp(x_i - m) in (0,1], no overflow; softmax invariant to additive shift. A correct.

B: unstructured sparsity rarely helps wall-clock on GPU unless density is very low. C: 2:4 structured sparsity is HW-accelerated, real 2x on tensor cores. D: for LLM decode, HBM-reducing sparse formats help because decode is BW-bound. A wrong: no automatic proportional speedup.
SwiGLU has 3 linear layers (gate, up, down) — 3*D*F params vs 2*D*F. To match parameter budget of a 2-linear MLP at intermediate dim F, SwiGLU uses (2/3)*F. A correct.
Standard two-stage GPU top-k: per-block top-k with in-register heap or bitonic, then merge. O(V log k) work. A correct.
